The main risk is therefore not that skew always worsens
fairness, but that it makes fairness assessment less stable and
predictable. When root data guides aggregation, demographic
coverage and sensitive-group balance should be treated as
explicit defense assumptions, and the fairness budget B should
be set according to the requirements of the target learning task.
B. Opportunity Offered by Synthetic Root Data
Beyond distributional bias, obtaining clean server-side root
data is a practical challenge for root-data-based FL defenses.
In decentralized FL, it is often unrealistic to assume that the
server can collect a large, representative, and trustworthy root
dataset. Even a root set comprising 5–10% of the overall
training data can be costly to acquire in practice. This chal-
lenge also creates an opportunity for synthetic augmentation.
Fairness-aware FL is commonly evaluated on tabular data with
explicit sensitive attributes, for which statistical generative
models are particularly suitable. Statistical generative methods
can model tabular distributions and generate samples that
retain key properties of the original data, offering a practical
way to augment a small clean root set.
To examine this opportunity, we vary the amount of clean
root data and employ different synthetic data generation meth-
ods, including CTGAN [37], FD [38], GC [39], PCA [40],
SMOTE [41], and TVAE [37], to augment the root dataset
to 10% of the overall training data. These methods include
distribution-based generators, such as CTGAN, TVAE, Forest-
Diffusion (FD), Gaussian Copula (GC), and a PCA based
method, which generate new samples by modeling the underly-
ing structure of tabular data, as well as the interpolation-based
SMOTE method for synthetic oversampling. Fig. 3 presents
the results under S-DFA. For visualization, we summarize
group fairness using
FairScore = 1 −(AEOD + ASPD)
(32)
where higher values indicate lower combined disparity.
The results show that lightweight root-data construction
can support a competitive utility–fairness trade-off. In Fig. 3,
configurations using synthetic augmentation generally lie near
the upper-right corner, which corresponds to high ACC and
FairScore. Several synthetic configurations match or improve
on the baseline using 10% real root data; for example, SMOTE
and TVAE yield favorable trade-offs on COMPAS with the
configuration using 1% real and 9% synthetic data. These
findings suggest that synthetic augmentation can complement
a small clean root set and reduce the practical burden of
collecting sufficient clean data for robust and fair aggregation.

C. Future Work
The root dataset is both a potential vulnerability and an
opportunity for robust and fairness-aware FL. A biased root
dataset can cause the server to underestimate or misinterpret
group-level risks, whereas a small but representative clean
root set augmented with suitable synthetic samples can still
provide useful signals for robust and fair aggregation. Root-
data construction, auditing, and augmentation should therefore
be treated as core design considerations rather than auxiliary
implementation choices. Future work should extend root-data-
assisted defenses beyond the tabular setting considered here
to image, text, and multimodal FL. It should also investigate
fairness-aware synthesis methods for complex and multi-
valued sensitive attributes.
VIII. CONCLUSION
This work introduces the Dual-Facet Attack (DFA), which
jointly targets predictive utility and group fairness in federated
learning. The mini-benchmark shows that existing fair, robust,
adaptive, and hybrid FL methods often fail to protect both
objectives simultaneously. To address this gap, we propose
GuardFed, which evaluates client updates using root utility,
update reliability, and fairness risk, and converts these signals
